assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, turn atoms in a lattice into a many-body frequency reference at the 10^-18 level. This is precision atomic physics at its best: a clear idea, a decisive experiment, and a thorough understanding of every systematic shift. It opens tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: The magic-wavelength concept is Katori's. Jun Ye's group brought the clocks to the highest accuracy and stability and added many-body (spin-exchange) physics. Two laureates fit cleanly and the supplied credit supports a coherent two-person configuration. Frequency combs were already recognised in 2005 (Hall and Hansch), and Ye's work builds on that.
assessment.maturity: Strong. Several independent laboratories worldwide (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL and others) have reproduced and improved the clocks, and clock comparisons agree. The interpretation is stable and the timing is ripe.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as one discovery or an extended programme of engineering improvements is a judgement call.
Competing clock platforms (single-ion clocks, partly recognised in 2012 via Wineland) could complicate how the prize is framed. I have not independently verified every priority detail.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Strongly interacting Fermi gases and the BEC-BCS crossover give a clean, tunable laboratory for pairing and superfluidity in the unitary regime. They connect to neutron stars and high-Tc superconductivity through universality. It is a fundamentally new regime where theory and experiment can be compared quantitatively (equation of state, pair condensation, sound).
assessment.attribution: Molecular BEC from fermions (Grimm, also Jin and Ketterle) and the crossover studies (Grimm, Salomon, Ketterle) are the decisive experiments. Deborah Jin, who played a central role, died in 2016 and is not among the credited names. Ketterle already holds a 2001 prize, so I propose Grimm and Salomon. A full allocation remains delicate.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The results were reproduced by many groups (Innsbruck, ENS, MIT, Duke, Rice, JILA) and the equation of state is well established. About two decades have passed, so timing is fine.
uncertainties: Attribution is difficult since Deborah Jin cannot be recognised posthumously.
Whether an earlier laureate such as Ketterle should be included is an open committee question.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard models with tunable parameters, show the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition, and now allow single-site imaging with quantum gas microscopes. This gives quantum simulation of many-body physics that classical computers handle poorly, with real insight into correlations and dynamics.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation; Greiner and Bloch carried out the Mott-insulator experiment and the microscopy work. Cirac is a major theorist but I would not use him twice across lists. Bloch, Greiner and Zoller is a plausible triplet from the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Strong. The platform is reproduced worldwide and has produced many quantitative comparisons with theory. Some later claims about quantum advantage in simulation are still developing.
uncertainties: Overlap with B009 and B047 through Zoller and Cirac makes the allocation of credit uncertain.
Greiner's contribution is split between the Mott experiment (done in Munich) and later microscopy at Harvard.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED brings cavity QED to superconducting circuits, with strong coupling, dispersive readout and the transmon-based architecture. It is the working basis of superconducting quantum processors. The scientific content is clear and sound, although it lies partly in engineering and is close to the 2025 prize topic (macroscopic quantum effects in circuits).
assessment.attribution: Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf proposed and demonstrated strong coupling in 2004, and the Yale group (Schoelkopf) also developed the transmon. Koch and others are significant for the transmon but are not credited here. The three-name configuration is reasonable, though Devoret's recognition in 2025 must be weighed.
assessment.maturity: Quite strong. The architecture is used by many laboratories and companies and the results are repeatedly confirmed. Recognition so soon after the 2025 prize may be seen as premature or redundant.
uncertainties: The 2025 prize to Clarke, Devoret and Martinis may make a second superconducting-circuit prize unlikely soon.
Credit among the cavity-QED idea, the transmon and the readout is shared with people outside the credited list.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal and its realisation with trapped ions (gates, entanglement, teleportation, error-corrected operations) established the first physical route to quantum computation. It is a fundamental demonstration of controlled many-body quantum states, building on ion trapping and laser cooling, which were recognised earlier (Paul 1989, Wineland 2012).
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the proposal. Blatt's Innsbruck group made decisive demonstrations, although Wineland's NIST group (already recognised) and others also contributed. Three names fit the supplied credit. Zoller also appears in B032, so the committee would need to decide how to allocate him.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the sense of repeated reproduction by several groups. Timing is acceptable, though the 2012 prize reduces the novelty.
uncertainties: The 2012 prize already honoured quantum control of individual ions.
Duplicate Zoller and Cirac credit across B009, B032 and B047 may need to be resolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum control of mechanical motion (ground-state cooling, squeezing, entanglement of mechanical oscillators) pushes the quantum-classical boundary to massive objects. This speaks directly to the question of where the quantum world ends. It is conceptually attractive, but the demonstrations are comparatively recent and have not yet had a transformative scientific use.
assessment.attribution: Cleland (quantum ground state of a mechanical resonator, 2010), Teufel (sideband cooling, squeezing) and Aspelmeyer (optomechanics foundations and entanglement) are strong. Kippenberg and Painter are equally important, and the limit of three laureates is hard to apply with five credited names, so allocation is the main problem.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature. Several groups have confirmed the results, but the field is still developing and overlaps in spirit with the 2025 prize.
uncertainties: Five credited names but at most three laureates, with no principled way to pick.
The field may be premature, and its benefit remains mostly demonstrative.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators opened a new class of phases of matter defined by topology rather than symmetry breaking, with experimental confirmation in HgTe wells and 3D materials. It is a major conceptual advance, but I defer to my condensed-matter colleagues on its ranking.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the theoretical proposals, and Molenkamp's group did the HgTe observation after the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, whose authors are not credited here. Hasan's ARPES work on 3D topological insulators is also important. The credit is difficult to confine to three people.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with many independent confirmations. It is in the topological-matter tradition already recognised in 2016, which slightly weakens novelty.
uncertainties: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and Hasan, cannot all be included in a three-person set.
I am less qualified to judge condensed-matter priority and rely on colleagues.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: X-ray free-electron lasers (SASE concept and its realisation at LCLS and European XFEL) give femtosecond coherent X-ray pulses and open time-resolved structural and atomic physics, including inner-shell dynamics familiar to me from theory. The value as an enabling instrument is large, but it is more an invention than a new physical insight.
assessment.attribution: Pellegrini, Kim and Rossbach are plausible originators of the concepts (SASE, high-gain theory, FLASH), although the allocation among accelerator physicists and later facility builders is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Mature technology with many facilities worldwide. Timing is acceptable, but the Nobel record for accelerator instruments is mixed.
uncertainties: I am not certain of the exact attribution history of the SASE concept.
The committee may treat it as a technical achievement rather than a discovery.
